Chapter 6: The Paradox of Effort—Trying Without Striving.
You know, there’s this quiet tension that shows up whenever we try to improve ourselves. On one side, there’s that real urge to grow—to feel more peaceful, stay focused, and maybe even become a little more awake to life.
But here’s the catch: it’s so easy to turn even the most heartfelt spiritual practice into just another task—something we feel we have to conquer, perfect, or tick off our never-ending to-do list.
In Zen, this whole paradox gets met with a kind of gentle smile. You walk the path with sincerity, sure, but without clinging or pushing too hard.
Imagine this: you sit down to meditate after a long, stressful day, hoping the practice will bring some relief—maybe even a breakthrough. At first, there’s a lot of effort. You try to sit up straight, breathe deeply, and do everything “right.”
But have you noticed what happens? The harder you try, the more restless your mind gets. Frustration sneaks in, and suddenly, giving up feels very tempting.
It’s right in these moments that non-striving starts to make sense. Meditation isn’t about forcing your mind to be still, or chasing after a certain feeling. It’s about just showing up, with your whole heart, and letting go of what you think should happen.
The real effort? It’s in the returning. It’s the willingness to start again—no matter how many times your mind wanders, or your legs go numb.
Most of us don’t realize how quickly effort can turn into self-judgment. The mind starts whispering, “You’re not doing enough,” or, “You should be better at this by now.” But here’s something to pay attention to—the invitation is to meet those thoughts with kindness. Notice them, let them be part of the scenery, and keep going.
Over time, you’ll notice that the deepest changes don’t come from forcing things, but from this gentle, steady persistence.
And this paradox isn’t just for meditation. You’ll see it in your work, your relationships, your creative life. Real progress usually happens when you strike a balance between intention and ease.
Think about a musician who practices scales—not to show off, but to really get to know their instrument. Or a parent listening to a child—not to fix things, but to understand. The effort is there, but it’s not heavy-handed or tense.
